prompt: A GPU has 16384 MiB of VRAM, and the desktop already uses 1536 MiB of it. You load a model with 48 transformer layers of 290 MiB each, plus a 410 MiB embedding/output block that must sit on the GPU. The KV cache needs 96 KiB per token of context and you want an 8192-token context; the whole KV cache and a 600 MiB compute buffer must also sit on the GPU. Whole layers are placed on the GPU until the next one would not fit; the rest go to system RAM. How many of the 48 layers end up on the GPU? Give a whole number.
solution:
free = 16384 - 1536
kv = 8192 * 96 / 1024          # MiB
left = free - 410 - kv - 600
layers = min(48, int(left // 290))
print(layers)

prompt: An API key has a monthly budget of $50.00. Every day the automation sends 0.9 million input tokens and 0.11 million output tokens, the same each day, starting from $0 spent on day 1. 40% of the input tokens are cache reads billed at 10% of the normal input price; the other input tokens cost $3.00 per million; output tokens cost $15.00 per million. At the end of which day of the month is the cumulative spend first above $50.00? Answer with the day number.
solution:
from fractions import Fraction as F
inp, out = F(9, 10), F(11, 100)
daily = inp * F(6, 10) * 3 + inp * F(4, 10) * F(3, 10) + out * 15
spent, day = F(0), 0
while spent <= 50:
    day += 1
    spent += daily
print(day)

prompt: A batch job sends 340 prompts to a local model one after another. Each prompt has 1500 prompt tokens and produces 420 output tokens. The model processes prompt tokens at 2400 tokens/s and generates output at 65 tokens/s, and every request also has 0.35 s of fixed overhead. How many minutes does the whole batch take? Give the answer to 2 decimal places.
solution:
per = 1500 / 2400 + 420 / 65 + 0.35
total_min = 340 * per / 60
print(f"{total_min:.2f}")

prompt: A script hands out ports to new services. It walks the candidates 11434, 11437, 11440, ... (each 3 more than the last), skips any candidate that is divisible by 7, and also skips 11443 and 11455 because they are already in use. The candidates that remain are given to 10 services in order. What port does the tenth service get?

Estimate the disk space for a set of quantized models. Each model's size in GB (1 GB = 10^9 bytes) is parameters x bits-per-weight / 8, and the whole set then needs 2% extra for metadata. The set: a 14.8-billion-parameter model at 4.5 bits per weight, the same 14.8-billion-parameter model again at 8.5 bits per weight, a 9.2-billion model at 4.5 bits, a 1.5-billion model at 4.85 bits, and a 137-million-parameter embedding model at 16 bits. What is the total in GB? Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

A GPU draws 285 W while generating and 22 W the rest of the time. It generates at 98 tokens/s, and every day it produces 1.9 million tokens; it is idle for the rest of each 24-hour day. Electricity costs $0.142 per kWh. What does the GPU's electricity cost over a 30-day month, in dollars? Give the answer to 2 decimal places.
solution:
gen_h = 1.9e6 / 98 / 3600
idle_h = 24 - gen_h
kwh_day = (285 * gen_h + 22 * idle_h) / 1000
print(f"{kwh_day * 30 * 0.142:.2f}")
rationale: Generation takes 5.386 h a day; 1.944 kWh a day; 58.33 kWh x $0.142 = $8.28.

prompt: Six services start one at a time: ollama, litellm, postgres, grafana, prometheus and webui. postgres starts before litellm. litellm starts before webui. prometheus and ollama start one right after the other (in either order). grafana starts neither first nor last. ollama does not start first. prometheus starts before postgres. grafana starts after litellm. Which service starts fourth? Answer with its name.
solution:
from itertools import permutations
names = ["ollama", "litellm", "postgres", "grafana", "prometheus", "webui"]
found = []
for order in permutations(names):
    p = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(order)}
    if (p["postgres"] < p["litellm"] < p["webui"]
            and abs(p["prometheus"] - p["ollama"]) == 1
            and p["grafana"] not in (0, 5)
            and p["ollama"] != 0
            and p["prometheus"] < p["postgres"]
            and p["grafana"] > p["litellm"]):
        found.append(order)
assert len(found) == 1, found
print(found[0][3])
rationale: The only order is prometheus, ollama, postgres, litellm, grafana, webui.

prompt: Four metrics exporters, A, B, C and D, each either always tells the truth or always lies. A says: "Exactly one of the four of us is truthful." B says: "A is a liar." C says: "B and D are of different kinds." D says: "Neither B nor C is truthful." Which exporters are truthful? Give their letters in alphabetical order with no spaces or separators (for example AD).
solution:
from itertools import product
found = []
for a, b, c, d in product([True, False], repeat=4):
    said = [sum([a, b, c, d]) == 1, not a, b != d, not b and not c]
    if [a, b, c, d] == said:
        found.append("".join(n for n, v in zip("ABCD", [a, b, c, d]) if v))
assert len(found) == 1, found
print(found[0])

prompt: Six models must each be placed on exactly one of three GPUs: X (24 GB), Y (16 GB) and Z (12 GB). The models are alpha 14 GB, bravo 10 GB, charlie 9 GB, delta 7 GB, echo 5 GB and foxtrot 3 GB. The models on a GPU may not add up to more than its memory. charlie and delta are on different GPUs. alpha and bravo are on different GPUs. alpha and delta are on the same GPU. Z holds exactly two models. Which GPU holds echo? Answer with its letter.

Six maintenance jobs (backup, prune, update, bench, report and rotate) run on six different days, Monday through Saturday, one job per day. prune runs the day immediately after backup. update runs on an earlier day than bench. report runs neither on Monday nor on Saturday. report runs on an earlier day than update. rotate runs on an earlier day than backup. bench does not run on Saturday. On which day does update run? Answer with the weekday name.
solution:
from itertools import permutations
days = ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday"]
jobs = ["backup", "prune", "update", "bench", "report", "rotate"]
found = []
for p in permutations(range(6)):
    d = dict(zip(jobs, p))
    if (d["prune"] == d["backup"] + 1 and d["update"] < d["bench"]
            and d["report"] not in (0, 5) and d["report"] < d["update"]
            and d["rotate"] < d["backup"] and d["bench"] != 5):
        found.append(d)
assert len(found) == 1, found
print(days[found[0]["update"]])

prompt: A migration has seven steps, A to G, run one at a time. A must come before B and before C. B and C must both come before D. C must come before E, and E before F. D and F must both come before G. How many different orders of the seven steps satisfy every rule?
solution:
from itertools import permutations
rules = [("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("C", "E"), ("E", "F"),
         ("D", "G"), ("F", "G")]
n = 0
for order in permutations("ABCDEFG"):
    pos = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(order)}
    n += all(pos[x] < pos[y] for x, y in rules)
print(n)

prompt: A service listens on a four-digit port between 8000 and 8999. Its four digits are all different, they add up to 26, its last digit is odd, and the port number is divisible by 7. What is the port?
solution:
found = [p for p in range(8000, 9000)
         if len(set(str(p))) == 4 and sum(map(int, str(p))) == 26
         and p % 2 == 1 and p % 7 == 0]
assert len(found) == 1, found
print(found[0])

prompt: A systemd timer on a server fires every day at 01:30 UTC. An operator in New York reads the logs in local time (America/New_York: EST is UTC-5 and EDT is UTC-4; in 2026 daylight time begins at 02:00 local time on Sunday 8 March). What New York wall-clock time does the run on 9 March 2026 (UTC date) show? Answer as HH:MM in 24-hour time.
solution:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
run = datetime(2026, 3, 9, 1, 30, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
print(run.astimezone(ZoneInfo("America/New_York")).strftime("%H:%M"))
rationale: The UTC run on 9 March is the evening of 8 March in New York, after the switch to EDT.

prompt: A log rotator writes one log file per day and, in addition, one weekly summary file on every Sunday. Files are kept for every date from 2026-02-20 through 2026-03-05, both ends included. 20 February 2026 is a Friday. How many files are kept in total?
solution:
from datetime import date, timedelta
d, end, n = date(2026, 2, 20), date(2026, 3, 5), 0
while d <= end:
    n += 1 + (d.weekday() == 6)
    d += timedelta(days=1)
print(n)
rationale: 14 dates (2026 is not a leap year) plus Sundays 22 Feb and 1 Mar.

prompt: A certificate is issued on Friday 2026-11-27 and expires 90 days after its issue date. A renewal timer runs every Monday and every Thursday, and the certificate is renewed at the first run that falls on or after the date 30 days before the expiry date. On what date is it renewed? Answer as YYYY-MM-DD.
solution:
from datetime import date, timedelta
expiry = date(2026, 11, 27) + timedelta(days=90)
d = expiry - timedelta(days=30)
while d.weekday() not in (0, 3):
    d += timedelta(days=1)
print(d.isoformat())
rationale: Expiry 2027-02-25; 30 days before is Tuesday 2027-01-26; next Monday/Thursday is Thursday 28 January.

prompt: You copy a 109 GiB model store over a network link whose line rate is 250 Mbit/s (1 Mbit = 10^6 bits; 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes). Protocol overhead takes 6% of the line rate, so data moves at 94% of it. How many minutes does the copy take? Give the answer to 2 decimal places.
solution:
bits = 109 * 2**30 * 8
seconds = bits / (250e6 * 0.94)
print(f"{seconds / 60:.2f}")

prompt: Two consecutive log lines come from a server in America/Chicago on 2026-11-01, the night daylight time ends: at 02:00 CDT the clocks go back to 01:00 CST (CDT is UTC-5, CST is UTC-6). The first line is stamped 01:45:00 CDT and the next 01:10:00 CST. How many minutes passed between the two lines?
solution:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
cdt, cst = timezone(timedelta(hours=-5)), timezone(timedelta(hours=-6))
a = datetime(2026, 11, 1, 1, 45, tzinfo=cdt)
b = datetime(2026, 11, 1, 1, 10, tzinfo=cst)
print(int((b - a).total_seconds() // 60))
rationale: 01:45 CDT is 06:45 UTC and 01:10 CST is 07:10 UTC.

prompt: A cron job has the schedule `*/20 9-17 * * 1-5`: at minutes 0, 20 and 40 of every hour from 09 through 17 inclusive, Monday to Friday. November 2026 has 30 days and starts on a Sunday. How many times does the job run in November 2026?
solution:
from datetime import date, timedelta
n, d = 0, date(2026, 11, 1)
while d.month == 11:
    if d.weekday() < 5:
        n += sum(1 for h in range(9, 18) for m in range(0, 60, 20))
    d += timedelta(days=1)
print(n)
rationale: 21 weekdays x 9 hours x 3 runs.

```python
print(sum(out))
```
solution:

prompt:
What does this bash script print when run with bash (default options)?

```bash
n=0
for f in a b "c d"; do n=$((n+1)); done
printf '%s\n' x y z | while read -r l; do n=$((n+10)); done
echo $((n * 2))
```
solution:
import subprocess
SCRIPT = 'n=0\nfor f in a b "c d"; do n=$((n+1)); done\nprintf \'%s\\n\' x y z | while read -r l; do n=$((n+10)); done\necho $((n * 2))'
r = subprocess.run(['bash', '-c', SCRIPT], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
print(r.stdout.strip())
rationale: The quoted "c d" is one word, and the while loop runs in a pipeline subshell.

prompt:
What does this Python 3 program print?

```python
fs = [lambda x, i=i: x + i for i in range(3)] + [lambda x: x * j for j in range(1, 3)]
print(sum(f(5) for f in fs))
```
solution:
fs = [lambda x, i=i: x + i for i in range(3)] + [lambda x: x * j for j in range(1, 3)]
print(sum(f(5) for f in fs))
rationale: Defaults bind i at creation (5+6+7); the last two closures see j=2 (10+10).

prompt: Rebuilding a server takes these tasks, with as many people as you like working in parallel. A: provision the host, 3 h. B: install the GPU driver, 2 h, after A. C: restore the databases, 4 h, after A. D: pull the models, 5 h, after B, and it cannot start until 1 h after B finishes (the host reboots). E: start the gateway, 1 h, after both C and D. F: import dashboards, 2 h, after C. G: smoke test, 1 h, after both E and F. What is the earliest time, in hours from the start, at which everything is done?

Two technicians share nine tasks. Each task needs one technician for its whole duration without interruption, a technician does one task at a time, and a task can start only once all of its prerequisites have finished. Tasks (hours, prerequisites): A 6 (none); B 5 (none); C 4 (after A); D 3 (after A and B); E 4 (after B); F 5 (after C and D); G 4 (after E); H 3 (after F and G); I 3 (after D). What is the smallest number of hours in which all nine tasks can be finished?
rationale: 37 h of work and an 18 h critical path, but the precedence forces idle time: 20 h.

prompt: You can keep 14.5 GB of models resident on a GPU. Each candidate model has a size and the number of requests per hour it would serve from VRAM: coder-14b 9.0 GB, 120; gemma-9b 5.4 GB, 70; r1-14b 9.0 GB, 60; coder-1.5b 1.0 GB, 45; embed 0.3 GB, 30; phi-3b 2.8 GB, 40; llama-8b 4.9 GB, 55. Choose a set of models whose sizes add up to at most 14.5 GB. What is the largest total requests per hour such a set can serve?
rationale: gemma-9b + llama-8b + phi-3b + coder-1.5b + embed = 14.4 GB, 240/h; taking coder-14b first tops out at 235.

prompt: A month needs 40 million input tokens and 6 million output tokens. You must pick exactly one cloud plan. Plan X: pay as you go, $0.30 per million input and $1.20 per million output. Plan Y: $15 a month including 30 million input and 3 million output tokens, then $0.25 per million input and $1.00 per million output beyond that. Plan Z: $40 a month including 60 million input and 10 million output tokens. You may also move traffic to a local GPU in whole millions of tokens (input or output), up to 20 million tokens in total per month, costing $0.04 per million tokens in electricity; the cloud plan carries the rest. What is the lowest possible monthly cost in dollars? Give the answer to 2 decimal places.
rationale: Plan X with all 6M output and 14M input moved local: 26 x 0.30 + 20 x 0.04 = 8.60.

prompt: A GPU can hold at most two models at a time and starts empty. Requests arrive in this order, each needing its model resident: A B C A B D A C B A D C. Loading a model counts as one load; when the GPU is full you choose which resident model to evict, and you know the whole sequence in advance. What is the smallest possible number of loads?

Seven backup archives must be copied whole onto 1000 GB drives (an archive cannot be split across drives). Their sizes are 600, 600, 600, 420, 420, 300 and 50 GB. What is the smallest number of drives needed?
rationale: The total (2990 GB) suggests 3, but no 420 fits beside a 600, so the two 420s need a fourth drive.
